buildings.name: Hand Mill
buildings.description: The simplest millstone, grinding grain into flour by hand.
buildings.flavor: Grinding grain between stones needs no engine, only a heavy upper stone and a hand to turn it. Hand mills appear wherever people cultivate grain, from the river valleys of South Asia to the highlands of the Americas, and remained in use long after larger mills existed. The small mill lets a household do without the workshop down the road.

buildings.name: Animal Mill
buildings.description: A mill that uses draft animals to turn the millstones.
buildings.flavor: Once draft animals were trained to walk a circle, the same millstones could be turned without human effort. The animal mill carries a heavier stone than the hand mill and frees the household's time for other work. It is a change of power, not of the principle of grinding.

buildings.name: Water Mill
buildings.description: A mill that uses water to set the millstones in motion.
buildings.flavor: A wheel in a stream turns the grindstone without tiring people or animals, but it needs a channel and a fall of water. Water mills were built in many regions, from the valleys of China to the river towns of the Middle East, wherever a reliable current could be led to the stone. The mill ties the town's bread to the rhythm of the water.

buildings.name: Windmill
buildings.description: A mill whose cloth sails catch the wind to turn two sets of millstones without needing running water.
buildings.flavor: Where water is scarce but wind is steady, sails can drive the same millstones. The cloth sail is light, cheap to replace and quick to mend, so a windmill can stand where a water wheel cannot. Its two sets of stones let one building serve more than one batch of grain.

buildings.name: Bakery
buildings.description: Bakes bread from flour, the staple of the city diet.
buildings.flavor: Bread needs only flour, water and fire, yet keeping a steady oven hot is work in itself. Communal ovens are known from the earliest farming towns in many parts of the world; a bakery makes that shared hearth a permanent place in the city. It turns the staple grain into a food that travels and keeps.

buildings.name: Slaughterhouse
buildings.description: Butchers livestock for meat, hides and bones to feed the city's crafts.
buildings.flavor: Butchery is as old as domestication: once animals are kept for milk or wool, their meat, hide and bones must eventually be processed. A slaughterhouse gathers that work in one place so that nothing of the animal is wasted. It links the pasture to the tanner, the soap maker and the kitchen.

buildings.name: Dairy
buildings.description: Turns milk into cheese, a good that keeps for a long time.
buildings.flavor: Milk spoils quickly, but cheese and other cultured milk foods keep for months. Herders developed the techniques independently from the steppes to the highlands of East Africa. A dairy makes those keeping qualities available to the whole town.

buildings.name: Charcoal Kiln
buildings.description: Burns wood or bamboo in a sealed kiln to produce charcoal.
buildings.flavor: Wood burns hotter and cleaner when it is first turned to charcoal in a sealed kiln. The operation is simple enough to be known wherever wood was plentiful, and it made metalworking possible with a small amount of fuel. A kiln turns a bulky forest product into one a smith can carry.

buildings.name: Coke Oven
buildings.description: Bakes coal without air in a sealed brick kiln to drive off smoke and sulfur, leaving hard metallurgical coke.
buildings.flavor: Coal can be cleaned of smoke and sulfur by heating it without air, much as wood is turned to charcoal. The resulting coke burns hot enough to reduce iron ore in a shaft furnace. That is why the coke oven belongs to the age of large-scale metal production rather than the first forge.

buildings.name: Forge
buildings.description: Blacksmiths forge metal tools and goods here.
buildings.flavor: A forge is where heated metal is shaped by hammering. It needs a hearth, a hammer and a worker who knows when the metal is soft enough — knowledge passed on in every metalworking tradition. The tools made here are what all the other crafts depend on.

buildings.name: Smithing Workshop
buildings.description: A water wheel drives the workshop hammer.
buildings.flavor: A water-driven hammer strikes without tiring a smith, so larger pieces of metal can be worked in one session. It is the same principle as the water mill, applied to a hammer instead of a grindstone. The workshop lets one smith do the work of several.

buildings.name: Smelter
buildings.description: Smelts metal ores into metal for the forge.
buildings.flavor: Ore is not yet metal: it must be heated with fuel until the metal separates from the rock. Smelting is known from very early metalworking cultures in Africa, Asia and the Americas, each with its own furnace design. A smelter repeats that transformation day after day.

buildings.name: Bloomery
buildings.description: Smelts iron ore into metal for the forge.
buildings.flavor: A bloomery reduces iron ore below the melting point, leaving a spongy mass of iron that is hammered into shape. Furnaces of this kind were built across many regions, from the Andes to West Africa and East Asia. They supply metal before a taller furnace becomes possible.

buildings.name: Blast Furnace
buildings.description: A tall shaft furnace that smelts iron ore with limestone or lime flux into molten cast iron.
buildings.flavor: A tall shaft furnace reaches the temperature at which iron melts, so the metal can be tapped as a liquid and cast. It needs a steady blast of air, a charge of ore and flux, and a furnace that stands repeated heat. The blast furnace turns iron from a craft material into a bulk one.

buildings.name: Potter's House
buildings.description: Makes clay pots, bricks and tablets on the potter's wheel.
buildings.flavor: The potter's wheel shapes clay faster and more evenly than hands alone. Wheels were used in many ancient centres of pottery, from the Yangtze valley to the Near East, and the potter's house turns that skill into the vessels the town needs. Fired clay also gives the builder brick and tile.

buildings.name: Pottery Workshop
buildings.description: Fires clay vessels, bricks and tablets in a high-temperature kiln.
buildings.flavor: A kiln that holds a steady, fierce fire turns a household craft into a workshop trade. Such kilns were built in East Asia and West Asia, where potters learned to read the flame and mix mineral glazes; better draught and a charge that does not spoil let one potter fire far more ware in a day.

buildings.name: Mason's Workshop
buildings.description: Works stone into hewn blocks and stone goods for construction.
buildings.flavor: Stone must be cut to size before it can be built into a wall. A workshop with chisels and a yard for blocks lets one mason prepare stone for many building sites. Since stone is heavy, the work is done as near the quarry and the town as possible.

buildings.name: Builder's Yard
buildings.description: The yard where builders keep their tools and binders and direct the work on the city's buildings.
buildings.flavor: A building site needs a place where the crew gathers, the tools are kept and the binder is mixed before it is carried to the wall. Such yards appear wherever towns build in stone or brick, from the Nile valley to the cities of Asia and the Andes. A builder here does not make a good for the warehouse: the work is the faster raising of every building in the city.

buildings.name: Tanner's House
buildings.description: Tans hides and sews leather goods.
buildings.flavor: A hide left untreated soon decays; tanning with bark or other plant matter turns it into leather that lasts. The craft is found wherever animals are raised, from the steppes to the savannas. The tanner's house supplies shoes, straps and covers to the rest of the city.

buildings.name: Tanner's Workshop
buildings.description: Tans and finishes leather and sews leather goods.
buildings.flavor: Separate vats and workbenches let tanners prepare hides and finish fine leather alongside their other work.

buildings.name: Weaver's House
buildings.description: A loom for weaving cloth, clothes and carpets from fibers.
buildings.flavor: A loom turns thread into cloth, crossing one thread after another. Simple looms were known to farmers and herders in many regions — flax in the north, cotton in South Asia, ramie in East Asia, wool on the steppes. The house keeps that daily work inside the town.

buildings.name: Weaver's Workshop
buildings.description: Horizontal foot-treadle looms weave different batches in parallel.
buildings.flavor: A foot treadle lifts the shed of the loom, leaving both hands free to pass the shuttle. Several such looms under one roof let different cloths be woven at the same time. The workshop increases output without changing the fibre or the weave.

buildings.name: Brewer's House
buildings.description: Brews various low-alcohol drinks by fermentation.
buildings.flavor: Fermentation turns grain into a low-alcohol drink that keeps better than the mash it came from. Brewing is known in many farming societies, from the Nile valley to the highlands of East Africa and the valleys of Asia. The brewer uses the same grain the miller and the baker use.

buildings.name: Fermentation Workshop
buildings.description: Large wooden vats hold separate batches of fermenting drink or vinegar.
buildings.flavor: Large vats let several batches ferment at once, each with its own time and temperature. The vessels are simple, but the workshop needs a worker who can judge when a batch is ready. The same skill turns the drink into vinegar when it is left too long.

buildings.name: Winemaker's House
buildings.description: Produces wine from grapes or fruit.
buildings.flavor: Grapes begin to ferment on their own once their skins are broken, so pressing is the oldest part of the craft. Vineyards and wild grapes are found in many climates, and the drink travelled far beyond the region where the fruit grew. The winemaker's house turns a perishable harvest into a good that can be stored.

buildings.name: Oilmaker's House
buildings.description: Presses vegetable oil out of oil crops.
buildings.flavor: The seeds of many plants hold oil that can be pressed out with a simple lever or wedge. Sesame in Africa and Asia, olives around the Mediterranean, and oil crops of the Americas all gave rise to the same craft. The house supplies cooking fat, the base for soap and fuel for lamps.

buildings.name: Oil Mill
buildings.description: Wedge presses squeeze oil from batches of oil crops.
buildings.flavor: A wedge press applies more force than a hand can, so more oil is recovered from the same batch of seed. The mill keeps several presses at work, each serving a batch of its own. It is the workshop version of the operation the oilmaker's house performs.

buildings.name: Glassmaker's House
buildings.description: Fuses glass and blows glassware.
buildings.flavor: Glass is made by melting sand with a flux, and it can be blown into shape while hot. The craft appeared in several ancient regions and travelled with the workers who knew the recipe. A glassmaker's house gives the town vessels and glassware that clay and wood cannot.

buildings.name: Glass Workshop
buildings.description: Spins molten glass into a flat crown and cuts it into window panes.
buildings.flavor: The glass workshop takes the melt a step beyond blowing vessels. A worker gathers a gob, blows it into a globe, transfers it to a pontil rod and sets it spinning in the furnace until centrifugal force opens it into a great flat disc. Radial cuts turn the disc into a stack of clear window panes. The craft needs a steady furnace and a steady hand, and it gives the town the glass that lets daylight into the walls of its buildings.

buildings.name: Optical Workshop
buildings.description: Grinds and polishes clear glass into lenses, magnifying glasses and spectacles.
buildings.flavor: A lens is a curve ground so exactly that it bends light to a point. In the optical workshop, clear glass is cut, ground against abrasives and polished until a curved face magnifies, focuses or corrects; the craft needs a steady hand and a patient eye, and it turns a piece of glass into the instrument that lets a scholar read what the unaided eye cannot.

buildings.name: Ropemaker's House
buildings.description: A workshop for twisting ropes and cables.
buildings.flavor: Rope is made by twisting fibres together; the twist is what gives a bundle of strands its strength. Fibres differ by region — hemp, flax, jute, agave — but the operation is the same. Every ship, well and building site needs the product of this house.

buildings.name: Ropewalk
buildings.description: Strands laid along a long covered lane are twisted into full-length ropes and cables.
buildings.flavor: A long covered lane lets a worker twist a rope to its full length in one pass. The building is long, but the tools are simple, and the result is a cable strong enough for a sail or a hoist. A ropewalk supplies the shipyard and the windmill alike.

buildings.name: Tar Distillery
buildings.description: Handles every step of making tar and tarring materials.
buildings.flavor: Tar and pitch are made by heating resinous wood until the tar runs out. The same product sealed boats and roofs in many regions, from the northern forests to the pine woods of the Americas. The distillery gathers the whole process in one workshop.

buildings.name: Soapmaker's House
buildings.description: Makes soap from vegetable oil and soda.
buildings.flavor: Soap is made by combining fat with alkali, and both are at hand wherever animals are rendered and soda or ash is available. The recipe was known in ancient Mesopotamia, in Egypt and in many later traditions. The house turns otherwise useless scraps into a good the whole town uses.

buildings.name: Silkmaker's House
buildings.description: Produces silk cloth.
buildings.flavor: Silk comes from the cocoon of a moth, which must be reeled before the insect breaks it. Sericulture began in East Asia and spread through trade to other regions; raising the worms and weaving the thread are two different crafts. The house turns that thread into cloth.

buildings.name: Kiln
buildings.description: Processes minerals into lime, gypsum plaster and alum, and prepares lime mortar and concrete in the kiln yard.
buildings.flavor: Limestone heated in a kiln becomes quicklime. In the surrounding yard, workers slake the lime and mix it with sand for mortar, or with reactive volcanic material and stone aggregate for concrete. Firing and mixing are separate operations within the same works. The kiln also processes gypsum and alunite into materials for other workshops.

buildings.name: Papyrus Workshop
buildings.description: Produces papyrus and other goods from papyrus stems.
buildings.flavor: Papyrus is made by laying strips of the reed's stem in crossing layers and pressing them into a sheet. The craft is tied to a plant that grows in warm wetlands and gave writing a light, cheap surface. The workshop turns a water plant into the material of records.

buildings.name: Smokehouse
buildings.description: Produces smoked fish.
buildings.flavor: Smoking preserves fish by drying it and coating it with compounds from the smoke. Coastal and river peoples in many regions developed the practice long before refrigeration. The smokehouse lets the catch of a good season last into a lean one.

buildings.name: Parchment Workshop
buildings.description: Produces parchment.
buildings.flavor: Parchment is made from animal skin that has been scraped, soaked and stretched. Unlike papyrus, it can be made wherever livestock are raised, which is why it became a writing surface in many different regions. The workshop supplies sheets that stand up to frequent use and travel.

buildings.name: Bookbinder's Workshop
buildings.description: Sews sheets of parchment or paper into books under a leather cover.
buildings.flavor: Loose sheets are easily lost; stitched under a cover, they become a book that can be carried and kept. The technique developed wherever paper or parchment was in use, from East Asian bindings to the codex of the Mediterranean. The binder turns writing into a durable object.

buildings.name: Library
buildings.description: A collection of written works, where scholars produce science.
buildings.flavor: A library is more than a store of sheets: it keeps knowledge available to people who did not write it themselves. Collections were gathered by temples, palaces and scholars in many parts of the world. In the town, the library is where written knowledge becomes science.

buildings.name: Carpenter's Workshop
buildings.description: Saws timber into planks for construction and crafts.
buildings.flavor: A saw turns a log into planks, which are easier to carry and build with than the whole trunk. Woodworking is among the oldest crafts, since wood is abundant and easy to shape. The workshop supplies every other trade that needs timber.

buildings.name: Market
buildings.description: A city building for trade. Building it unlocks the transition to the Antiquity era.
buildings.flavor: A market is a place where goods change hands regularly rather than by chance encounter. Such meeting places exist in every farming society, from the highlands of the Americas to the river towns of Asia and Africa. The town's market turns trade into a lasting institution.

buildings.name: Mint
buildings.description: Strikes the city's coins out of copper, silver or gold, and takes a seigniorage on every batch.
buildings.flavor: A coin is a piece of metal of a known weight and mark, which saves weighing it at every exchange. Striking coins needs a die, a hammer and a ruler whose mark is trusted. The mint gives the town's trade a measure that travels beyond it.

buildings.name: Tax Yard
buildings.description: The yard where the dues of the citizens are tallied, weighed and carried into the treasury.
buildings.flavor: A tax must be counted, stored and carried somewhere before it can pay for anything. Keeping the dues in one yard makes that work visible and gives the treasury a predictable income. Tax systems appear wherever a city has expenses no single household can meet.

buildings.name: Paper Workshop
buildings.description: Makes paper.
buildings.flavor: Paper begins as plant fibre beaten into pulp and dried into thin sheets. The craft began in East Asia and reached other regions over centuries of trade; almost any fibre-rich plant can serve as raw material. A paper workshop gives writing a surface cheaper than parchment.

buildings.name: Paper Mill
buildings.description: Water-driven stampers beat plant fibres into pulp for paper.
buildings.flavor: Water-driven stampers beat fibre into pulp far faster than hands can, so a mill can keep several batches in production. The principle is the same as in the water mill and the fulling of cloth, applied to a different material. The mill makes paper a bulk good.

buildings.name: Dryer's House
buildings.description: Dries and cures various goods.
buildings.flavor: Sun and air preserve food by removing the water that spoilage needs. Drying is among the oldest methods of preservation: fruit, grain, fish and herbs were dried in every climate with a dry season. The dryer's house makes that method available whatever the weather outside.

buildings.name: Tobacco Workshop
buildings.description: Cures and cuts tobacco leaf.
buildings.flavor: Tobacco was first used by the peoples of the Americas, long before it reached other continents. The leaf is cured and cut before it is smoked or prepared in other ways. The workshop turns a raw crop into a good the citizens can use.

buildings.name: Scriptorium
buildings.description: A building where scribes copy, rewrite and translate documents. Produces science.
buildings.flavor: A scriptorium is a room set aside for copying and correcting texts. Scribes worked in palaces, temples and monasteries in many regions; their careful copies carried much of the ancient world's writing to later generations. Here that work produces science for the town.

buildings.name: University
buildings.description: A place where scholars teach and study, turning written knowledge into science.
buildings.flavor: A university is not a larger scriptorium: the work changes from copying what was written to teaching it and asking what else might be true. Houses of higher learning took different names in different regions — academies, madrasas, monastery schools, guilds of masters — but each kept texts, teachers and pupils together in one place.

buildings.name: Dyer's House
buildings.description: A building where dyes are extracted from all sorts of organic and inorganic materials.
buildings.flavor: Colour can be fixed into cloth with plant matter, minerals and a mordant. Dyeing traditions developed independently wherever textiles were woven, using local plants and minerals. The dyer's house gives the weaver's product its final value.

buildings.name: Jeweler's House
buildings.description: A building where jewelry is made from all sorts of materials.
buildings.flavor: Metal and stone can be worked into ornaments that carry meaning beyond their weight. Jewellers used whatever their region supplied — gold, silver, copper, shell, jade — so the craft never depended on one material. The house turns valuable raw goods into objects the town can keep or trade.

buildings.name: Alchemist's House
buildings.description: A building where alchemists run all kinds of chemical reactions.
buildings.flavor: Before chemistry had a name, workers heated, dissolved and combined substances in search of useful transformations. The tradition drew on metalworking, medicine and dyeing in many regions. The alchemist's house is where such experiments are carried out deliberately.

buildings.name: Cooper's House
buildings.description: A building where cooper makes barrels and other containers.
buildings.flavor: A barrel is made of staves held by hoops: the shape is strong, stackable and easy to roll. Coopering spread wherever goods had to be carried in bulk, from wine and oil to grain and tar. The cooper's house supplies the containers other workshops cannot do without.

buildings.name: Perfumer's House
buildings.description: Grinds aromatic resins into perfumes and incense.
buildings.flavor: Aromatic resins, flowers and spices can be ground, mixed and burned to give a scent. Perfumes and incense were made in many ancient cultures, from East Asia to the Mediterranean and the Americas. The house works the raw resin into goods worth more than the material itself.

buildings.name: Sugar Boiler
buildings.description: Boils a sweet juice down to sugar.
buildings.flavor: Sugarcane was cultivated in South and Southeast Asia long before sugar reached other regions; beet and other sweet plants later gave the craft a second source. Boiling the juice drives off water so that sugar can be stored and carried. The sugar boiler turns a bulky juice into a compact sweet.

buildings.name: Furniture Maker's House
buildings.description: A building where a furniture maker crafts furniture and luxury furniture from wood.
buildings.flavor: Wood can be joined into a chair, a chest or a table as well as cut into planks. Furniture traditions differ widely — low stools, raised beds, folding screens — but the joinery answers the same needs. The house makes the town's homes usable and, at its best, luxurious.

buildings.name: Distillery
buildings.description: Distils fermented drinks and sweet mashes into strong spirits, rectified spirit and fragrant cordials.
buildings.flavor: Distillation separates a volatile liquid from a fermented mash by boiling it and cooling the vapour. The technique is known in many traditions, from the Near East to the highlands of the Americas, and serves medicine as well as drink. The distillery carries it out on a scale a household cannot.

buildings.name: Chandler's House
buildings.description: Dips rendered tallow and moulds beeswax into candles for households, mines and workshops.
buildings.flavor: A candle is fuel given a shape so that it burns slowly: tallow from rendered fat or wax from a hive. Candle-making existed wherever those materials were at hand, and light after dark extended the working day. The chandler supplies mines, workshops and homes.

buildings.name: Sailmaker's Workshop
buildings.description: Weaves, cuts and dresses heavy canvas for boat sails and windmill sweeps.
buildings.flavor: A sail is a piece of cloth cut and reinforced so that the wind can pull a boat. The craft grew with sailing itself, in every region where boats moved people and goods, and later served the windmill as well. The sailmaker turns woven canvas into power.

buildings.name: Boatyard
buildings.description: Builds sturdy wooden boats rigged with cloth sails and rope.
buildings.flavor: A wooden boat needs a frame, planking and a way to seal the seams, all of which a yard can keep in repair. Boatbuilding traditions arose independently on rivers, lakes and coasts across the world. The yard builds the hull; the sailmaker and the ropemaker supply the rest.
